packages.name: EMSCodeSim Demonstration Protocol Pack
packages.sourceLabel: Demonstration content — compare every item with your current agency protocol

drills.title: Adult respiratory distress
objectives: Recognize signs of inadequate ventilation and rapid deterioration.
Match interventions to patient presentation and local scope.
Identify the reassessment findings that should change the plan.

review.appliesWhen: An adult has increased work of breathing, abnormal respiratory rate or effort, hypoxia, abnormal breath sounds, or inability to speak normally.
keyAssessment: Airway patency, respiratory rate, depth, effort, speech, chest movement, and mental status
Pulse oximetry and capnography when available and authorized
Breath sounds before and after treatment
History of asthma, COPD, heart failure, allergies, medications, and recent illness
actions: Position the patient, support the airway, and provide oxygen or ventilation based on clinical need.
Use the treatment pathway and medications authorized by the selected local protocol.
Reassess work of breathing, mental status, vital signs, and response after every intervention.
stopPoints: Do not delay assisted ventilation in a tiring or poorly ventilating patient.
Confirm local contraindications before CPAP or medication administration.
medicalControl: Contact medical control when required by protocol, when the patient falls outside standing orders, or when response is poor.
transport: Choose destination and urgency based on severity, response, airway risk, and local transport policy.

scenario.dispatch: Difficulty breathing at a private residence.
scenario.patient: A 68-year-old is seated upright, speaking in two- to three-word sentences, and becoming tired. Breath sounds are diminished with diffuse wheezing.
scenario.prompt: Which action best reflects the immediate protocol priority?

choices.text: Complete a detailed history before providing respiratory support
choices.feedback: A detailed history matters, but respiratory support and rapid assessment should not be delayed in a tiring patient.

choices.text: Support airway and ventilation, begin indicated treatment, and reassess continuously
choices.feedback: This keeps immediate threats, treatment, and reassessment connected.

choices.text: Wait for a complete set of vital signs before deciding whether the patient is severe
choices.feedback: The visible work of breathing and fatigue already require immediate action.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests impending respiratory failure?
options: Increasing fatigue and reduced air movement
questions.rationale: Fatigue and reduced air movement can indicate that the patient is no longer maintaining effective ventilation.

questions.question: What should happen after each respiratory intervention?
options: Reassess breathing, mental status, vital signs, and treatment response
Document only if the treatment failed
questions.rationale: Reassessment determines whether the patient is improving, unchanged, or deteriorating.

questions.question: Which source controls the exact medication, CPAP, and medical-control requirements?
options: The current local protocol and medical direction
The last partner you worked with
questions.rationale: Local protocol, scope, and medical direction control the exact treatment pathway.

actions: Identify ventilation failure early.
Treat within local scope without delaying basic support.
Reassess after every intervention.
summary.mistake: Focusing on a diagnosis while missing worsening ventilation.
summary.control: Use medical control whenever the local protocol requires it or the patient is outside standing orders.
summary.documentation: Record baseline severity, treatment, response, repeat findings, and transport decision.

drills.title: Suspected acute coronary syndrome
objectives: Identify high-risk chest-discomfort presentations.
Review medication contraindication checks.
Connect early assessment with destination and transport urgency.

review.appliesWhen: An adult has chest pressure, discomfort, anginal equivalent symptoms, unexplained dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, syncope, or other findings concerning for cardiac ischemia.
keyAssessment: OPQRST and SAMPLE history
Blood pressure, perfusion, lung sounds, and oxygenation
Medication history and contraindications
12-lead acquisition and transmission when authorized
actions: Treat immediate threats and minimize exertion.
Follow local medication and ECG pathways.
Select destination and notification based on local STEMI and cardiac destination policy.
stopPoints: Do not administer medication until the required contraindications and vital-sign limits are checked.
Do not let a normal-looking patient or atypical symptom pattern remove cardiac concern.
medicalControl: Contact medical control when required for medication, borderline findings, destination questions, or deviation from standing orders.
transport: Avoid unnecessary delay when time-sensitive cardiac disease is possible.

scenario.patient: A 59-year-old reports pressure with nausea and sweating. The patient appears pale and has not yet provided a complete medication history.
scenario.prompt: What should happen before a protocol-directed medication is given?

choices.text: Confirm the required indication, contraindications, medication history, and vital-sign limits
choices.feedback: Medication safety requires the checks specified by the current local protocol.

choices.text: Give the medication immediately because the complaint is chest pain
choices.feedback: The complaint alone does not replace contraindication and vital-sign checks.

choices.text: Delay all care until a complete written history is available
choices.feedback: Immediate assessment and supportive care can proceed while the history is gathered.

questions.question: Which symptom can be an anginal equivalent?
questions.rationale: Cardiac ischemia may present without classic chest pain.

questions.question: What determines exact medication eligibility?
options: Local protocol indications, contraindications, and vital-sign limits
questions.rationale: The local medication protocol defines required safety checks.

questions.question: Why is early destination planning important?
options: It can reduce delay to time-sensitive cardiac care
It eliminates the need for a handoff
questions.rationale: Destination decisions can affect time to definitive cardiac care.

actions: Recognize atypical as well as classic presentations.
Check every medication requirement.
Plan time-sensitive transport early.
summary.mistake: Treating the complaint label instead of the patient and contraindications.
summary.control: Clarify medication or destination uncertainty through the required medical-control pathway.
summary.documentation: Document symptoms, required checks, serial findings, treatment response, and notifications.

drills.title: Suspected stroke and destination decision
objectives: Establish last known well accurately.
Use the locally required stroke screen and severity tool.
Apply destination and notification rules.

review.appliesWhen: A patient has new facial weakness, arm drift, speech change, vision change, severe imbalance, focal deficit, or unexplained altered mental status.
keyAssessment: Exact last known well and symptom discovery time
Blood glucose and stroke mimic assessment
Local stroke screen and severity score
Airway, oxygenation, blood pressure, anticoagulant history, and baseline function
actions: Correct immediate threats and check blood glucose.
Complete the required local stroke assessment without creating scene delay.
Follow local destination, bypass, prenotification, and consultation rules.
stopPoints: Do not substitute symptom discovery time for last known well.
Do not allow an incomplete history to delay transport after immediate threats are addressed.
medicalControl: Use medical control for destination uncertainty or circumstances specified by protocol.
transport: Time, severity, geography, and local stroke-center policy guide destination.

scenario.dispatch: Possible stroke at an assisted-living facility.
scenario.patient: Staff found the patient with new speech difficulty at 0715. The patient was last observed normal during a 0600 medication pass.
scenario.prompt: Which time should be documented as last known well?

choices.text: 0715, when symptoms were discovered
choices.feedback: Discovery time and last known well are different when no one observed symptom onset.

choices.text: 0600, when the patient was last observed normal
choices.feedback: Last known well is the last time the patient was known to be at neurologic baseline.

choices.text: The time EMS arrived
choices.feedback: EMS arrival time does not establish last known well.

questions.question: Which bedside test is commonly required to evaluate an important stroke mimic?
questions.rationale: Abnormal blood glucose can mimic or complicate a stroke presentation.

questions.question: What should control bypass and destination decisions?
options: The closest hospital in every case
questions.rationale: Stroke systems and bypass criteria vary by region.

questions.question: Which is the best definition of last known well?
options: The last time the patient was known to be at neurologic baseline
questions.rationale: Last known well is based on the last confirmed normal neurologic state.

actions: Get an exact last known well.
Check glucose and complete the local stroke tool.
Use the regional destination and prenotification pathway.
summary.mistake: Recording symptom discovery as last known well without clarifying the timeline.
summary.control: Use the required consultation pathway when destination criteria are uncertain.
summary.documentation: Record baseline, last known well, discovery time, stroke findings, glucose, destination rationale, and notification.

drills.title: Patient refusal and high-risk non-transport
objectives: Separate decision-making capacity from simple orientation.
Identify high-risk refusal triggers.
Review documentation and consultation requirements.

review.appliesWhen: A patient declines assessment, treatment, transport, or a recommended destination.
keyAssessment: Immediate threats and decision-making capacity
Understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and ability to communicate a choice
Influence of intoxication, hypoxia, head injury, metabolic problem, or mental-health emergency
High-risk findings defined by local policy
actions: Explain findings, recommended care, material risks, and alternatives in understandable language.
Attempt reasonable problem-solving and involve appropriate supports.
Follow local medical-control, law-enforcement, supervisor, and documentation policy.
stopPoints: Orientation alone does not prove capacity.
A signature does not replace assessment, disclosure, consultation, or documentation.
medicalControl: Many systems require consultation for high-risk refusals, questionable capacity, minors, or specific clinical presentations.
transport: Offer transport again when new information or deterioration changes the risk discussion.

scenario.patient: The patient is oriented but repeatedly forgets what happened, cannot explain the risks of refusing, and wants to leave.
scenario.prompt: What is the most important next step?

choices.text: Accept the refusal because the patient knows name, place, and date
choices.feedback: Orientation is only one part of capacity and does not resolve the memory and reasoning concerns.

choices.text: Assess capacity more fully and follow the high-risk consultation pathway
choices.feedback: The patient may not be able to understand, appreciate, or reason through the decision.

choices.text: Ask for a signature and leave immediately
choices.feedback: A signature does not substitute for capacity assessment and required consultation.

questions.question: Which statement about decision-making capacity is most accurate?
options: Capacity includes understanding, appreciation, reasoning, and communicating a choice
questions.rationale: Capacity is decision-specific and requires more than orientation.

questions.question: What should be documented in a refusal?
options: Assessment, capacity, risks explained, alternatives, consultation, and return instructions
questions.rationale: A complete record supports patient safety and continuity.

questions.question: What determines when medical control is mandatory?
questions.rationale: Consultation requirements vary by system and risk category.

actions: Assess capacity, not just orientation.
Explain risks and alternatives clearly.
Follow local high-risk consultation and documentation rules.
summary.mistake: Using a signed form as a substitute for a clinical and capacity assessment.
summary.control: Know which refusal categories require medical control or supervisor involvement.
summary.documentation: Record findings, capacity elements, recommendations, risks, alternatives, witnesses, consultation, and instructions.

drills.title: CPAP application and monitoring
objectives: Confirm local indications and contraindications.
Apply the device while coaching the patient.
Recognize failure and the need to escalate ventilation support.

review.appliesWhen: A patient has significant respiratory distress and meets the local indication criteria for noninvasive positive-pressure support.
keyAssessment: Mental status and ability to protect the airway
Blood pressure and perfusion
Respiratory effort, oxygenation, and breath sounds
Vomiting risk, facial trauma, pneumothorax concern, and local contraindications
actions: Prepare equipment and explain the procedure.
Apply the mask, begin at the locally approved setting, coach the patient, and secure the seal.
Continuously monitor tolerance, airway, blood pressure, ventilation, and response.
stopPoints: Stop or escalate when the patient cannot protect the airway, becomes intolerant, deteriorates, or meets a local discontinuation criterion.
Be ready to provide assisted ventilation.
medicalControl: Follow local requirements for authorization, medication adjuncts, pressure changes, or failure.
transport: Do not let device setup create avoidable transport delay in a critically ill patient.

scenario.patient: The patient is alert and cooperative but has increasing work of breathing. You are preparing CPAP.
scenario.prompt: Which preparation is most important before the mask is applied?

choices.text: Confirm indications, contraindications, airway status, and ability to tolerate the device
choices.feedback: CPAP requires an appropriate patient and readiness to manage deterioration.

choices.text: Apply the mask before assessing mental status
choices.feedback: Mental status and airway protection are essential safety checks.

choices.text: Delay all monitoring until the patient adjusts to the mask
choices.feedback: Monitoring should continue during application and throughout use.

questions.question: Which finding may indicate CPAP failure?
options: Improved speech and lower work of breathing
questions.rationale: Worsening mental status and fatigue can indicate failure and a need for assisted ventilation.

questions.question: What should be monitored continuously?
options: Airway, mental status, blood pressure, ventilation, tolerance, and response
questions.rationale: CPAP can affect several systems and may fail despite one improving number.

questions.question: Where are the exact pressure settings and contraindications found?
options: The current local protocol and device guidance
questions.rationale: Settings and safety criteria must match local protocol and approved equipment guidance.

actions: Confirm the patient is appropriate.
Coach and monitor during application.
Recognize failure early and be ready to ventilate.
summary.mistake: Watching oxygen saturation while missing declining mental status or ventilation.
summary.control: Know local authorization, pressure-change, adjunct-medication, and failure requirements.
summary.documentation: Record pre-application findings, settings, tolerance, serial findings, and response.

drills.title: Bag-mask ventilation quality
objectives: Identify inadequate ventilation.
Prioritize airway positioning and mask seal.
Use visible chest rise and physiologic response to guide quality.

review.appliesWhen: A patient is apneic or breathing inadequately and requires positive-pressure ventilation.
keyAssessment: Airway patency and need for suction
Respiratory rate, depth, effort, chest movement, and mental status
Mask fit and facial anatomy
Oxygenation and capnography when available
actions: Open and clear the airway and insert an appropriate adjunct when indicated.
Use a two-person technique when resources allow.
Ventilate at the locally recommended rate and volume, using visible chest rise and avoiding excessive pressure.
stopPoints: Correct poor chest rise before simply squeezing harder.
medicalControl: Follow local escalation pathways when ventilation remains ineffective.
transport: Continue airway management and reassessment during movement and transport.

scenario.dispatch: Unresponsive person with slow, shallow breathing.
scenario.patient: Initial bag-mask ventilations produce little chest movement and significant resistance.

choices.text: Squeeze the bag harder and faster
choices.feedback: Excessive pressure and rate can worsen ventilation and increase complications.

choices.text: Reposition and clear the airway, improve the seal, and use a two-person technique
choices.feedback: Airway position, patency, and mask seal should be corrected before increasing pressure.

choices.text: Stop ventilating until a monitor is attached
choices.feedback: An inadequately breathing patient needs immediate ventilation support while monitoring is added.

questions.question: What is the best immediate visual indicator of an effective breath?
options: The mask makes a loud sound
questions.rationale: Visible chest rise helps guide appropriate breath delivery.

questions.question: Which technique generally improves mask seal and airway control?
questions.rationale: A two-person technique often improves seal and airway positioning.

questions.question: What should happen when chest rise is poor?
options: Correct position, patency, adjunct, seal, and technique
Ignore it if oxygen is connected
questions.rationale: Poor chest rise requires troubleshooting the airway and technique.

actions: Open and clear the airway.
Use the best seal and two-person technique available.
Ventilate to chest rise and reassess continuously.
summary.mistake: Compensating for a poor seal or obstructed airway by squeezing harder and faster.
summary.control: Follow local escalation and advanced-airway pathways when basic ventilation is ineffective.
summary.documentation: Record initial ventilation status, airway actions, technique, response, and monitoring.

drills.title: Adult tachycardia with a pulse
objectives: Identify instability based on the whole patient.
Separate immediate stabilization from rhythm classification.
Use the local synchronized-cardioversion and medication pathway.

review.appliesWhen: An adult has a persistent tachyarrhythmia with a pulse and clinical symptoms or instability.
keyAssessment: Airway, breathing, perfusion, mental status, chest discomfort, heart failure, and shock
Monitor rhythm and 12-lead when feasible without delaying urgent care
Potential causes and medication history
Whether the patient meets local instability criteria
actions: Treat immediate threats and determine stable versus unstable using local definitions.
Follow the local synchronized-cardioversion, sedation, and medication pathway.
Reassess rhythm and perfusion after every intervention.
stopPoints: Do not allow prolonged rhythm analysis to delay treatment of an unstable patient.
Confirm synchronization and local energy guidance before cardioversion.
medicalControl: Use medical control as required for medications, repeated therapy, unusual rhythms, or protocol variance.
transport: Coordinate urgent transport and destination based on response and local cardiac system policy.

scenario.patient: A patient has a rapid rhythm, altered mental status, cool skin, and weak pulses. The monitor is being attached.
scenario.prompt: Which principle should guide the next decision?

choices.text: Treat the patient as unstable and follow the immediate local tachycardia pathway
choices.feedback: Clinical instability should drive urgent treatment while rhythm information is obtained.

choices.text: Delay treatment until a perfect 12-lead is printed
choices.feedback: A 12-lead is useful but should not delay urgent care in an unstable patient.

choices.text: Assume every rapid rhythm receives the same medication
choices.feedback: Treatment depends on stability, rhythm characteristics, patient factors, and local protocol.

questions.question: Which finding supports instability?
options: Altered mental status with weak pulses
questions.rationale: Instability is determined by patient effects such as poor perfusion, altered mental status, ischemia, or heart failure.

questions.question: What must be confirmed before synchronized cardioversion?
options: That all vital signs are normal
Synchronization and the current local energy/sedation pathway
That the patient has no medical history
questions.rationale: Synchronization and local procedural guidance are critical safety elements.

questions.question: What follows every intervention?
questions.rationale: The rhythm and the patient's clinical response must both be reassessed.

actions: Define stability from the patient, not rate alone.
Do not delay urgent treatment for perfect diagnostics.
Reassess rhythm and perfusion after each action.
summary.mistake: Focusing on the monitor while missing worsening perfusion.
summary.control: Know the local cardioversion, sedation, medication, repeat-treatment, and consultation requirements.
summary.documentation: Record instability findings, rhythm interpretation, synchronized settings, medications, response, and consultation.

drills.title: Pediatric anaphylaxis
objectives: Recognize multisystem allergic emergencies.
Use weight-based medication safeguards.
Anticipate airway and perfusion deterioration.

review.appliesWhen: A child has a likely allergic exposure with airway, breathing, circulatory, or multisystem findings consistent with anaphylaxis.
keyAssessment: Airway swelling, voice change, stridor, wheezing, work of breathing, and oxygenation
Perfusion, mental status, skin findings, vomiting, and abdominal symptoms
Estimated or measured weight and medication concentration
Exposure, onset, prior reactions, and pre-arrival treatment
actions: Treat immediate airway, breathing, and perfusion threats.
Use the exact weight-based medication, concentration, route, and maximum in the current local protocol.
Prepare for rapid deterioration and reassess after each intervention.
stopPoints: Do not rely on skin findings alone to determine severity.
Complete an independent dose and concentration cross-check before administration whenever circumstances allow.
medicalControl: Follow local requirements for repeat medication, infusion therapy, refractory shock, or protocol variance.
transport: Use urgent transport and early destination notification for severe or refractory reactions.

scenario.dispatch: Child with allergic reaction after food exposure.
scenario.patient: The child has wheezing, facial swelling, vomiting, and poor perfusion. A caregiver reports a weight, but the medication concentration has not been confirmed.

choices.text: Use the adult amount because the child appears critically ill
choices.feedback: Severity does not remove pediatric weight and concentration safeguards.

choices.text: Confirm weight, indication, concentration, route, calculated dose, and local maximum
choices.feedback: This structured cross-check reduces pediatric medication error.

choices.text: Wait for skin findings to worsen before treating
choices.feedback: The child already has respiratory, gastrointestinal, and perfusion involvement.

questions.question: Why can anaphylaxis be present without dramatic hives?
options: Skin findings are required in every case
Airway, breathing, circulatory, or multisystem findings may predominate
questions.rationale: Severe anaphylaxis may be recognized through airway, breathing, circulation, and multisystem findings even when skin findings are limited.

questions.question: Which pediatric medication check is most complete?
options: Weight, indication, concentration, route, calculated dose, maximum, and independent check
questions.rationale: A complete cross-check reduces concentration and calculation errors.

questions.question: What should happen after medication is given?
options: Reassess airway, breathing, perfusion, mental status, and need for repeat therapy
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis can recur or progress and requires close reassessment.

actions: Recognize multisystem disease early.
Use a complete pediatric dose/concentration check.
Prepare for airway and shock deterioration.
summary.mistake: Waiting for dramatic skin findings or skipping the concentration check in a critical child.
summary.control: Know local repeat-dose, infusion, refractory-shock, and consultation requirements.
summary.documentation: Record exposure, weight source, concentration, calculation, dose, route, time, serial response, and consultation.
